title: Chesterton's fairyland
hook: Chesterton, in Orthodoxy (1908), argues life is a strange gift like a fairy tale

segments.voice: Yesterday, Soloviev, who longed for the churches of East and West to be one again. Your line was all one. Who got your kind word across a divide? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

Why is grass green? A small child asks, and the grown-up has an answer ready. Then the child asks why again, and again, and before long the grown-up runs out and says: it just is. The English writer G. K. Chesterton thought that last answer deserved a much longer look. In his book Orthodoxy there's a chapter called The Ethics of Elfland, and it starts in the nursery, with the fairy tales of his childhood. Those stories, he says, taught him something about the real world that grown-up books had missed. Today, Chesterton's fairyland.

In fairyland, nobody pretends a golden apple had to be golden. It's magic: someone chose it. Chesterton turns that around on the world outside the window. We say it's a law that apples fall and leaves are green, and the word law makes it sound necessary, as if it couldn't have been any other way. But we don't actually know why it's this way and not another. It's as surprising as anything in a fairy tale. A world where grass happens to be green is a world someone might have chosen. Then he goes a step further. We tend to think repetition means something is dead, like a machine. Chesterton suggests the opposite. A laughing child says "Do it again!" and means it every single time. Perhaps, he says, God makes each daisy separately and has never grown tired of making them, with the strength of a child who wants the same game over and over. Jesus pointed somewhere nearby: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." And the psalmist, looking out at creation, doesn't explain it at all. He marvels: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Chesterton's point isn't that the world is a fable. It's that the world is stranger than a fable, and that being alive at all is a gift nobody earned. And a gift, he says, leaves you wanting someone to thank.
screen: `FAIRYLAND: SOMEONE CHOSE IT` · `A LAW, OR A KIND OF MAGIC?` · `DO IT AGAIN` · `A GIFT WANTS SOMEONE TO THANK`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wonder at something ordinary. Settle, and breathe. Pick one plain thing within reach: a spoon, a key, the grain of a table, a slice of bread. Look at it as if you'd stepped into a story and this was the first one you'd ever seen. Why this color? Why this shape? Why is it here at all? Don't answer. Let it be strange for a while. If you pray, you can borrow the psalmist's line: O Lord, how manifold are thy works. The bell holds the time.
Chesterton's fairyland. G. K. Chesterton's idea that the ordinary world is as strange and chosen as a fairy tale, and calls for thanks.

Your line: the world is strange. That closes a week of thinkers: Wesley's warm heart, Schleiermacher's dependence, Kierkegaard's individual, Newman's seed, Khomiakov's sobornost, Soloviev's reunion, and Chesterton's wonder. Today, look twice at one thing you see every day. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians who love Chesterton often read Orthodoxy as a book of gratitude and wonder rather than argument alone; churches also give thanks for creation in their prayers, and some Christians say grace before meals.
